newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu vows to hold chunk of West Bank forever.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu vows to hold chunk of West Bank forever.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, even as the Arab League held an emergency session on his settlement policies, vowed on Sunday that the Jordan Valley area of the occupied West Bank would be part of Israel forever.

"The prime minister met today with representatives of the Jordan Valley...In the meeting the prime minister said that the government saw the Jordan Valley as inseparable from the State of Israel in any permanent agreement," Netanyahu's office said in a statement issued to the media.
Netanyahu was quoted by the settlers as saying an additional 470 housing units for Jews would be built in the area.

The right-wing Netanyahu has enraged Palestinians and Arab states with his rejection of trading occupied land for peace, the key to peace deals cut by the centre-left government he ousted in May elections.

Netanyahu's office said it was checking the report on new housing construction. The statement it issued spoke of developing Jewish settlements in the area in general but did not specifically refer to building new housing units. It said:

"The prime minister said that the government has total commitment to the development and prosperity of the Jordan Valley and even in a tough budget year such as this the government will budget monies for the development of the infrastructure and roads in the Jordan Valley."
A spokeswoman for Jordan Valley Jewish settler leader David Levy said Netanyahu promised during the meeting to expand existing settlements in the area.
"Four hundred and seventy in the Jordan Valley and Maale Ephraim," spokeswoman Tami Atia told Reuters. Maale Ephraim is situated in the cliffs overlooking the valley.
The Jordan river is the border between the West Bank, which Israel captured in the 1967 Middle East war, and Jordan.

Israel's late prime minister Yitzhak Rabin, assassinated one year ago by a right-wing Jew, said Israel's "security border" would remain the Jordan river valley portion of the West Bank. Netanyahu's formulation is less vague.

The Arab League met in Cairo on Sunday at the request of the Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) to discuss Netanyahu's settlement expansion policy and Middle East peace moves that have stalled since Netanyahu took office in June.
The PLO told the Arab League Israel's policies would reignite violence in the region and isolate the Jewish state.

"Israel insists on ripping apart the West Bank to prevent the creation of a Palestinian state, but we are determined to defend our lands by all possible means against racist settlement plans," the Palestinian representative added.
Netanyahu opposes a Palestinian state.

Final status peace talks -- to deal with issues like settlements, the nature of the final Palestinian political entity, and refugees -- were launched in May before Israel's elections. They have yet to resume under Netanyahu.
The PLO set up autonomous enclaves in parts of the West Bank and Gaza Strip under an interim deal with Israel signed in 1993.
More than 130,000 Jews live amidst nearly two million Arabs in the West Bank and Gaza Strip.
After taking office in June, Netanyahu lifted a freeze on settlement building imposed by the previous government.
Israel's Peace Now movement, which monitors settlement, says Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai, who gives final approval for new building, has approved 3,000 new West Bank homes.
Mordechai's office refuses to say how many new units the government has approved.
